title: Dedicate, swap or share: placing twenty small models on GPUs, and a simulator that missed its own test
question: Twenty small models on rented RTX 4090s: dedicate a GPU to each, swap models through a shared pool, or co-locate two per GPU? Which is cheapest as popularity skew and arrival timing change? The answer comes from a simulator that failed its pre-registered [validation gate](p2:gate).

requirements.short: One sizing rule for all three
requirements.text: Size every strategy by the same rule: hot models pinned the same way, then the smallest fleet that meets the SLO.
requirements.why: If only some strategies may give a hot model extra GPUs, the rule, not the measurement, decides the high-skew result (scope amendment §7).

requirements.text: Hold the latency target for every popularity decile of models, not only for all requests together.
requirements.why: Popular models send most requests, so an aggregate [p99](p2:percentiles) can pass while some tenants fail (design §8).

requirements.text: Sweep popularity skew at two arrival regimes that give each model the same long-run share.
requirements.why: Swapping with LRU follows whether a model's requests come together in time, not how often they come; skew alone misses that (design §7).

requirements.text: Measure on the GPU what a swap, a co-located neighbour and a memory split cost; simulate only traffic, fleet dynamics and queueing.
requirements.why: Only the hardware can answer them; interference "cannot be reasoned to" (design, module 2).

requirements.short: Rules first; trust only after a gate
requirements.text: Fix the rules before the data is analysed, and record any later change as a dated [amendment](p2:amendment); trust the simulator only if it reproduces a real replay, and publish a miss.
requirements.why: Fleet numbers are a model's; only a test fixed in advance separates a finding from model error ([a failed gate is a result](p2:failed)).

requirements.text: State the result as a decision rule in GPUs and monthly dollars, with every conversion assumption published.
requirements.why: The portfolio requires money too, and readers must be able to substitute their own rate.

concepts.plain: The k-th most popular of 20 models gets a share proportional to 1 / k to the power s. Total load: one GPU's measured throughput, 8.89 requests per second. A model above 0.7 of a GPU is **hot** and gets pinned GPUs in every strategy (worked under Results).

Same long-run share per model, different timing. **Spread**: random (Poisson) arrivals, each labelled independently. **Bursty**: each model is ON in bursts of about 120 s, a fifth of the time. In a burst its load is five times its average, so the bursty hot-model rule uses that ON-period load.

Stop one [vLLM](p1:vllm) engine, wait for its memory to free, start the next model's engine until it answers health: median **37.8 s** over 16 warm swaps, [compile cache](p1:compile) hit. The swap strategy's pool evicts the **least recently used** model. Sleep mode (5.0 s) was measured, never simulated.

Two vLLM 0.27.1 engines on one card, 45% of its memory each. The [KV cache](p1:kvcache) falls from **168,464** tokens alone to **55,104** (pinned): room for 82 full-length requests of 2,048 tokens, against 26 (26 to 28 were seen running). That is 3.1 times less for a 2.0 times smaller share: about 2.6 from a fixed cost of roughly 3.6 GiB outside the KV cache, 1.18 from the pin (see the memory result).

**SLO: p99 at most 75.6 s**, twice the median swap. A **decile** is 2 of the 20 models by popularity. Its p99 is taken in each simulated run, then the median over 30 runs. A fleet size passes only if all ten deciles meet the SLO.

concepts.short: This gate: one GPU, three tenants
concepts.plain: Three tenants on **one GPU**, a 900 s bursty trace of 1,562 requests with real swaps, replayed **three times**. Per 30 s bin, the simulator's median latency must fall inside the three repeats' band. Pass: at least 10 judged bins, at most half missing, swap count within the real range ±1. Co-location gets only two **held-out** interference cells.

decisions.title: New fleet simulator
decisions.problem: The question is about fleets of 10 to 25 GPUs and 20 models; the August design planned to extend artifact 2's simulator.
options: Extend artifact 2's simulator with a model dimension (the August design)
Assume co-located models each get half the throughput
A new loop with GPU identity: route by residency, swap by LRU, serve every request; swap, interference and KV split measured
decisions.chosen: A new loop with GPU identity: route by residency, swap by LRU, serve every request; swap, interference and KV split measured
decisions.why: Artifact 2's loop has no replica identity, and placement is exactly which GPU holds which model; changing it would also change artifact 2's code mid-experiment. The half-the-throughput guess is "almost certainly wrong in both directions" (design), so it was measured. Every request is served, because dropping unfinished ones would drop the cold-tail requests stuck behind swaps.
decisions.why_short: Artifact 2's loop has no GPU identity, and placement is which GPU holds which model; the half-the-throughput guess had to be measured.
decisions.cost: A new loop to build. Service time is frozen at dispatch, capacity is the top measured concurrency, and neighbour load between 0 and 16 is interpolated, not measured.
decisions.cost_short: A new loop to build; service time frozen at dispatch; neighbour load 1 to 15 interpolated, not measured.

serves.because: The three primitives enter as measurements.

uses.because: A swap is a stall drawn from 16 measured swaps.
Co-located latency comes from the measured surface.

decisions.title: One sizing rule
decisions.problem: At equal GPU counts the strategies cost the same, so each needs its own fleet size, by a rule that cannot decide the result by itself.
options: Compare the strategies at one fixed number of GPUs
Let only some strategies replicate hot models
Size on the aggregate p99 of all requests
In the bursty regime, let every strategy search up to a common cap
One hot-model rule for all three; the smallest fleet whose every decile meets the SLO; bursty sizing on ON-period load
decisions.chosen: One hot-model rule for all three; the smallest fleet whose every decile meets the SLO; bursty sizing on ON-period load
decisions.why: Hot models get pinned GPUs in every strategy, so strategies differ only in how the rest are placed. The aggregate p99 is mostly popular models' requests, so it passes fleets that fail the hottest tenants (swap 9 GPUs, not 10; see How it works). On average load, a placeholder sweep left every bursty strategy dominated; the owner chose ON-period load.
decisions.why_short: Hot models are pinned alike in all three, and a fleet passes only if every decile meets the SLO: the aggregate hides the hottest tenants.
decisions.cost: Swap needs one GPU more at the reference point. Swap and co-locate search only up to dedicate's size, where their layouts become dedicate's, so dedicating can at best tie. Bursty s = 0.6 is not evaluable: a decile had too few requests for a p99.
decisions.cost_short: Swap needs a GPU more; dedicating can at best tie by construction; bursty s = 0.6 is not evaluable.

serves.because: Same hot-model rule and SLO search for all three.
All ten deciles must meet the SLO.
A sized fleet is a GPU count, priced at a published rate.

uses.because: The SLO is applied decile by decile.
Skew decides which models are hot.

decisions.title: Two arrival regimes
decisions.problem: Skew says how often each model is asked for, not whether its requests come together. Swapping by LRU depends on the second.
options: At each skew, a spread regime (independent arrivals) and a bursty one (ON about a fifth of the time, 120 s bursts), with identical long-run shares
decisions.chosen: At each skew, a spread regime (independent arrivals) and a bursty one (ON about a fifth of the time, 120 s bursts), with identical long-run shares
decisions.why: Both generators take the same shares, so only clustering in time differs; skew alone "would earn the correct objection that the analysis ignores locality" (design §7). The simulator put the boundary between the regimes, with no crossover along skew in either.
decisions.why_short: LRU swapping follows whether a model's requests cluster in time, not how often they come, so skew alone would miss the mechanism.
decisions.cost: Only two regimes were built, so the data cannot say where between them the winner changes. The gate's trace used a third shape (180 s bursts at duty 0.25).
decisions.cost_short: Only two regimes: the data cannot place the boundary between them.

uses.because: The two regimes differ only in timing.
Both regimes are swept over the same six skews.

decisions.title: Small model, KV that binds
decisions.problem: Two of artifact 1's 8B models (about 16 GB each) do not fit a 24 GB card, and at the earlier short request the KV cache never fills.
options: A different card for the co-location arm
Qwen3-4B, falling back to Qwen3-1.7B, by a go/no-go fixed before reconnaissance; a request long enough that the split's KV binds
decisions.chosen: Qwen3-4B, falling back to Qwen3-1.7B, by a go/no-go fixed before reconnaissance; a request long enough that the split's KV binds
decisions.why: A different card would confound strategy with hardware. Pass: both engines healthy at 45% of memory, each with at least 16,384 KV tokens. The 4B pair left 9,456 and 9,520; the 1.7B pair passed. The shape rule chose 1,792 input and 256 output tokens: a split engine has room for 26 full-length requests, a lone one for 82.
decisions.why_short: Two 8B models do not fit one card, and a short request never fills the KV cache; a go/no-go fixed in advance picked the size.
decisions.cost: A small-model result (3.8 GiB of weights); swap and co-location costs scale with size. Two warm engines did not fit at 45% each, so their KV was pinned to 55,104 tokens by a signed amendment.
decisions.cost_short: A small-model result, and the pair's KV had to be pinned by an amendment to fit at all.

serves.because: All three strategies fit one card class.
Criterion and fallback committed before reconnaissance.

uses.because: The shape makes the split's KV ceiling bind.

decisions.title: Ranking-blind load and SLO
decisions.problem: On placeholder inputs both regimes came out degenerate: the 4 s SLO was shorter than one swap. Load and SLO decide whether the strategies can differ at all.
options: Keep the placeholder design point (four GPUs of load, a 4 s SLO)
A screen over 3 loads × 3 SLO multiples of the swap median that scores how many strategies each grid point tells apart, never which is cheaper
decisions.chosen: A screen over 3 loads × 3 SLO multiples of the swap median that scores how many strategies each grid point tells apart, never which is cheaper
decisions.why: A count of distinct fleet sizes cannot favour a strategy. Ties went to the earlier candidate: one GPU of load and twice the swap median, 75.6 s with the measured swaps. The screen's data was committed before the values it set.
decisions.why_short: Counting how many strategies a point tells apart cannot favour one; the placeholder SLO was shorter than a swap.
decisions.cost: Twice a swap absorbs a swap, which favours swapping: at the reference point the simulated swap fleet delivers about 45 s p99, the others 4 to 5 s. The measured sweep ran at this one SLO, and the screen ran on placeholder engines. At twice a swap even the simulated spread swap pool at s = 1.0, which never finds a model resident (hit rate 0.0), meets the SLO: its worst decile is 74.3 s against 75.6.
decisions.cost_short: Twice a swap favours swapping, and the measured sweep ran at that one SLO.

serves.because: Rule fixed before reconnaissance, output before measuring.
One SLO and one load apply to all three strategies.

uses.because: The SLO is a multiple of the swap median.
The swap median sets the SLO's seconds.

decisions.title: One-GPU replay gate
decisions.problem: Fleet numbers mean something only if the simulator reproduces a real system; the design scaled artifact 2's gate down to one GPU.
options: Draw each predicted swap from the measured distribution
After the failure, re-validate with the swap time calibrated
Three real replays of one 900 s bursty trace; predict with the median measured swap; publish whatever the verdict
decisions.chosen: Three real replays of one 900 s bursty trace; predict with the median measured swap; publish whatever the verdict
decisions.why: A model cannot be held tighter than three real repeats' spread, and a fixed swap time keeps the prediction deterministic. It failed: 10 of 13 judged bins outside, always too slow. Recalibrating would not rescue it: charged each repeat's own swaps, 12 of 13 still miss, the other way.
decisions.why_short: Three real repeats set the tolerance and a fixed swap keeps the prediction deterministic; the verdict is published either way.
decisions.cost: No fleet size is validated: the gate tested one GPU, three tenants and swapping only, at a burst shape and load the sweep did not use; co-location had two held-out cells, one missed. The diagnosis is exploratory.
decisions.cost_short: Failed, so GPU counts are unvalidated; co-location was never replayed and one of two held-out cells missed.

serves.because: Rule fixed before the replays; the failed verdict stands.

uses.because: Three repeats, 30 s bins, at most half missing.
Each swap was charged the 37.8 s median.

results.title: UNVALIDATED: GPUs, spread arrivals

chart.y_label: GPUs to meet the SLO in every decile

results.axis: Simulated by a model that failed its gate. Swap: the smallest pool meeting the 75.6 s p99 SLO in every decile, 30 runs.
results.read_as: Co-locate is cheapest at every skew; dedicating, which can at best tie by construction, needs twice as many. Spread swap's peak at s = 1.25 was not diagnosed.
results.takeaway: In the simulator, how traffic arrives picks the winner, not skew. The ordering is wide; the counts are not validated.

chart.y_label: GPUs to meet the SLO in every decile
chart.note: SIMULATED, FAILED VALIDATION. Bursty s = 0.6 is not evaluable: some decile had too few requests for a p99 in some run.

results.axis: Dedicate is rule arithmetic; co-locate sits at its pairing floor, where the SLO held at every evaluable point.
results.read_as: Swap is cheapest at every evaluable skew; dedicating needs about twice as many.
results.arithmetic: Reference point, bursty s = 1.0: 21, 10, 12 GPUs. One GPU-month = $1.1095 × 730 h = $809.935; 21 × 809.935 / 20 tenants = $850.43; dedicate costs $8,909.28 a month more than swap.

results.title: Hot rule and floors
results.axis: Peak load = Zipf share × 1 GPU × 5 (bursty) or 1 (spread); the spread row spans s 0.6 to 2.0 and no model is hot. Hot above 0.7: pinned = ceil(load / 0.7) per hot model. Dedicate = pinned + rest; floor = pinned + half the rest, paired.
results.read_as: Spread never makes a model hot; co-locate searched but landed exactly on its floor everywhere, so only swap's size moved off a rule-given value.

results.title: Search ranges
results.axis: At s = 1.0. Whisker: the ladder the search may climb (not a confidence interval). Dot: the first size that met the SLO. Sizes come from the simulator that failed its gate.
results.read_as: Both ladders end at dedicate's placement, so dedicating can at best tie.

series.name: swap, 9 GPUs: sized on the aggregate p99

chart.note: SIMULATED, FAILED VALIDATION. Swap at the reference point, bursty s = 1.0.

results.axis: Simulated. Swap's p99 per decile at 9 GPUs (what an aggregate-p99 rule picks) and at 10 (the per-decile rule).
results.read_as: At 9 GPUs deciles 1 and 2 breach (87.7 and 77.2 s); the coldest does not. The design expected the cold tail to suffer; the post does not explain why the hottest do.

results.arithmetic: A decile is 2 of 20 models: each run's p99, then the median over 30 runs.

results.title: Memory: one engine, two
results.axis: Card 23.52 GiB. Fixed: budget minus KV cache, the [weights](p1:weights) among it. Pin give-up: (64,976 − 55,104 tokens) × 114,688 B. Bar 2 totals both engines; pin give-up is 1.054 GiB each. Subtractions, not measurements.
results.read_as: Unpinned, two warm engines failed in graph capture: the first held 11.84 GiB (budget 10.58), the second 11.16, the worker 0.5; 15 MiB were free when the second's graph capture asked for 20 MiB more. The pin (6,319,767,552 bytes of KV, 3,444 blocks) gives up about 1 GiB each. A memory fraction appears to budget one engine rather than partition the card (inferred; the 1.26 GiB over budget was not itemised).

results.title: Measured: busy neighbour, about 2× slower

chart.note: Held-out cells: own 24 with neighbour 48 (passed), own 48 with neighbour 24 (missed, above the split ceiling of 26). A cell passes if the prediction is inside its repeats' range or within 10% of their median.

results.axis: Measured on RunPod: median latency of 1,792 + 256-token requests, 3 or more runs per point. Split: two engines at 45% of memory, KV pinned to 55,104 tokens.
results.read_as: A busy neighbour makes a model 2.0 to 2.4 times slower at every load, even one request; 32 and 64 match because the neighbour sits at its ceiling. An idle neighbour costs nothing up to 32; at 64 the split engine is slower even alone (8.63 against 7.66 s), probably queueing behind its ceiling of 26.
results.takeaway: Next to a busy neighbour a model does slightly worse than half a card, and holds under a third of the requests it could alone.

results.title: Measured: where a 37.8 s swap goes
results.short: A swap is mostly process start
results.axis: Median seconds per stage. Swap: 16 warm swaps of Qwen3-1.7B. Cold start: artifact 1's arm C [cold start](p1:coldstart) (Qwen3-8B), a reference, not a baseline.
results.read_as: A swap skips platform scheduling and compiling (a cache hit) but re-pays process start, imports and the health check: 27.8 of 37.8 s. Artifact 1's launch segment is not a weight download: 16.7 of its 21.3 s is server start-up before the model-loading line (arm C medians), which a swap also pays.
results.takeaway: For a model this small, a swap is about as long as artifact 1's 8B cold start: process start dominates.
results.arithmetic: Stage medians: 0.8 + 0.04 + 27.8 + 2.2 + 6.8 + 0.3 = 37.94 s, not the 37.8 s median swap (medians do not add). Cold start: 4.8 + 21.3 + 8.6 + 4.1 + 0.3 = 39.1 s.

results.title: Pool thrash numbers
results.axis: At the sized swap fleet. Hit rate: arrivals that found their model resident, over all arrivals, pinned models included (bursty: about 0.75 for the pool's own models). Seconds between swaps, per pool GPU: pool × 3,600 / swaps per hour. A swap takes 37.8 s (median).
results.read_as: Same shares, different timing: a spread pool starts a swap every 43 s per GPU, a bursty pool every 298 s.

results.title: Gate failed: 10 of 13 bins miss

chart.x_label: start of 30 s bin, scheduled arrival (s)
chart.note: Judged bins only, rounded to whole seconds; 16 bins had too few requests to judge. The marker is the slowest repeat, the whisker runs to the fastest: that is the band the rule tests.

results.axis: One GPU, three tenants, a 900 s bursty trace with real swaps. Predicted: the simulator, every swap at 37.8 s. Real: three repeats on one pod.
results.read_as: All ten misses sit above the band: the simulator predicted the engine slower, by up to 67.8 s. Three late bins agree. The swap count agreed (11 against 10); the latency did not.

chart.x_label: busy-neighbour latency, times the measured (step surface)
chart.note: EXPLORATORY: one skew (s = 1.0), 6 runs, one SLO, after the analysis. The multipliers are not measurements.

interview.pitch30: I asked how to place twenty small LLMs on rented GPUs: a GPU each, a shared swap pool, or two per card. I measured what the hardware charges for a swap and for a busy neighbour, and fed that into a fleet simulator. Its answer: how traffic arrives picks the winner, not how skewed it is. Pair models when requests are spread out, swap when they come in bursts; dedicating, which by construction can at best tie, never won. But the simulator failed its own pre-registered test, 10 of 13 bins, so the GPU counts are unvalidated.
interview.pitch120: For 20 small models on RTX 4090s I compared dedicating a GPU each, swapping through a shared LRU pool, and co-locating two per GPU, across Zipf skew and two arrival patterns with the same per-model shares, spread and bursty. On the GPU I measured a swap (median 37.8 s, mostly process start), a busy neighbour (2.0 to 2.4 times slower) and the memory split (KV cache 168,464 down to 55,104 tokens). A new simulator sized each strategy to the smallest fleet where every popularity decile meets a 75.6 s p99; aggregate sizing would have let the hottest tenants breach. Simulated result: co-locate when spread, swap when bursty, dedicating about twice the cheapest. But my pre-registered gate, three real replays on one GPU, failed: 10 of 13 bins outside the band. An exploratory diagnosis found the simulator charged 37.8 s per swap where the replay pod took about 25 s, and even at that 12 of 13 still missed; the likely gap is a term for what a swap costs nearby requests, unmeasured. So the ordering is wide and the counts are unvalidated. The paid runs cost $25.23.

followups.q: Why trust a simulator that failed its gate?
followups.a: For GPU counts, I don't: the gate failed at its one point (one GPU, three tenants, swapping only), the fleets are 10 to 25 GPUs, and co-location had two held-out cells, one missed. The ordering is wide, about twice, but I did not test whether the model's error leaves it unchanged. The measured swap, slowdown and KV split stand.

Partly by construction: swap and co-locate search only up to dedicate's size, where their layouts become dedicate's, so dedicating can at best tie (scope amendment §7; the post does not say this). Only swap's count came from the SLO search (see How it works). The simulated margin is the point: co-locate's p99 of about 2 to 6 s met the 75.6 s SLO at half of dedicate's 20 GPUs.

Arrival timing (only two regimes built); the SLO (twice a swap favours swapping, and the sweep ran at one SLO); interference (exploratory: four times the busy-neighbour latency loses co-location the bursty regime, eight the spread one); model size (a 1.7B result).

Exploratory, after the verdict. A host up to 30% faster does not close it. The gate charged 37.8 s per swap; replay swaps took about 25 s. Charged that, the simulator is too fast and 12 of 13 bins still miss: probably it lacks a term for what a swap costs nearby requests, which I did not measure.

followups.q: You switched models and changed rules mid-campaign. Isn't that moving the goalposts?
followups.a: The 1.7B switch was a branch committed before reconnaissance. The KV pin came after the first co-located runs crashed, before any valid co-located data, confirmed by a probe and signed; the validity and ramp amendments came after the cell runs, before their analysis. All dated in git; the re-runs cost 7.45 unplanned GPU-hours.
Measure what a swap costs the requests around it, on one pod with the replay's own requests: the likely missing term. A recalibrated re-run would not pass. Co-location needs its own replay.

interview.limits: Every GPU count, dollar figure and the decision rule are from a simulator that failed its gate (10 of 13 bins; see What the gate covered). Whether the model's error leaves the ordering unchanged was not tested. Qwen3-1.7B, not the registered 4B; one size and request shape; LRU only; one GPU class and datacenter; warm swaps only; swap time varies about 50% by pod; one SLO, twice a swap, which favours swapping; two arrival regimes. Sleep mode measured, never simulated. The diagnosis and the interference sensitivity are exploratory. The post is an unpublished draft.

recall.q: Why can the strategies not be compared at the same number of GPUs?
recall.a: At equal counts they cost the same by construction. Each is sized to its smallest fleet meeting the SLO, and cost follows from that count.

recall.q: Spread and bursty traffic give each model the same share. What differs, and what does it change?
recall.a: Timing. In a burst one swap-in serves many requests; scattered, a model is loaded, evicted and loaded again (design module 4). Simulated: swap cheapest when bursty, co-locate when spread.

recall.q: At the reference point, what does sizing on the aggregate p99 get wrong?
recall.a: In the simulator it picks 9 GPUs for swap, and the two hottest deciles breach the SLO; per-decile sizing needs 10 (numbers in How it works). R2.

recall.q: Which cold-start stages does a swap skip, and what does it still pay?
recall.a: It skips platform scheduling and compiling (a cache hit). It re-pays process start, imports and the health check, 27.8 of 37.8 s.

recall.q: Splitting memory halves each engine's share. Why does its KV cache shrink 3.1 times?
recall.a: About 2.6 times is a fixed cost, roughly 3.6 GiB outside the KV cache at either budget, which comes off the smaller budget first. The other 1.18 is the pin to the compiled engine's 55,104 tokens, which lets two graph captures fit: 168,464 to 55,104 tokens, 82 to 26 requests.

recall.q: A busy neighbour makes a model about twice as slow. Why does co-locating still halve the simulated spread fleet?
recall.a: SLO headroom, not low load: about 2 to 6 s against 75.6 s. In the exploratory run it held at the worst reading of the unmeasured range.

recall.q: Why can dedicating at best tie under this sizing rule?
recall.a: Swap and co-locate search only up to dedicate's size, where their layouts become dedicate's and serve identically, so dedicating can tie but never win. The simulated margin is the point.

recall.q: The gate charged 37.8 s per swap; the replay pod's swaps took about 25 s. Why does charging 25 s not rescue the gate?
recall.a: Then it predicts faster than real and 12 of 13 bins still miss: no fixed swap cost matches. The exploratory diagnosis blames a missing term for a swap's effect on nearby requests, unmeasured.

recall.q: What did the gate test, and what did it never test?
recall.a: One GPU, three tenants, swapping, 180 s bursts at 0.3 of a GPU. Never co-location (two held-out cells), never a multi-GPU fleet or LRU victim choice across GPUs, never the swept 120 s bursts.

recall.q: Which requirement breaks if the GPU counts are presented as findings, and what may be said instead?
recall.a: R5. The ordering may be called wide but unvalidated; the measured primitives stand.

walkthrough.title: Where 21, 10 and 12 GPUs come from
walkthrough.lead: One reference point: bursty arrivals, Zipf s = 1.0, 20 models, one GPU of load. Dedicate's and co-locate's counts are arithmetic; swap's 10 and the SLO checks are simulated, by a simulator that failed its gate.

steps.say: Twenty models share one GPU's worth of load (8.89 req/s, one GPU's measured saturation), Zipf s = 1.0. Bursty: each model is ON about a fifth of the time, at five times its average load. No GPU is placed yet.
The [hot rule](a4:zipf): the top model has 0.278 of the traffic, so 1.39 GPU of load while ON. Over 0.7, so it gets ceil(1.39 / 0.7) = ceil(1.985) = 2 pinned GPUs, in every strategy (derived).

Model 2 has 0.139 of the traffic, 0.695 GPU while ON: 0.005 under 0.7, so not hot. A 0.69 threshold would pin 5 GPUs, not 2 (derived): the rule sets this edge, not the data. The other 18 models are lower still.
Dedicate: the pinned GPUs plus one GPU per tail model, 2 + 19 = 21 (derived). One placement, never searched.
Swap: the pinned GPUs plus a shared LRU pool grown from 1 to 19 GPUs, so 3 to 21 in all. Sizing takes the first count where all ten popularity deciles meet the 75.6 s p99 [SLO](a4:slo).
At 9 GPUs the two hottest deciles sit at 87.7 and 77.2 s, over the SLO. At 10 (a pool of 8) the worst decile is 56.8 s. So the first count to pass is 10 (simulated, median of 30 runs).

Co-locate: pinned GPUs plus the 19 tail models paired, 9 pairs and 1 single, so 12. Un-pairing adds GPUs up to 21. The first count tried, 12, already passed (worst decile 6.1 s, simulated): the pairing floor.
Both searches end at 21, so dedicate can tie but never win. Load used: 1/21 = 4.8%, 1/10 = 10%, 1/12 = 8.3% (derived). Models held set dedicate's and co-locate's counts; swap's comes from swap delay.

walkthrough.takeaway: Dedicate's 21 and co-locate's 12 follow from the hot rule and pairing; the simulator only showed the pairing floor passes the SLO (12 here; all 11 evaluable points). Only swap's 10 was searched. All unvalidated.
